claim: Neuroimaging studies have identified significant neural activity in the midline cerebellum during mental recall of emotional episodes.
source: Neuroimaging studies have identified significant neural activity in the midline cerebellum during mental recall of emotional episodes (Damasio et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Damasio et al., 2000

claim: Meta-analysis of patients with posttraumatic stress disorders (PTSD) has implicated the cerebellum as one of the activated regions during recall of traumatic memories.
source: The meta-analysis of patients with posttraumatic stress disorders (PTSD) has implicated the cerebellum as one of the activated regions during recall of traumatic memories (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2016

claim: Inactivation of the cerebellar vermis with tetrodotoxin disrupted fear memory consolidation in rodents.
source: In rodents, the inactivation of the cerebellar vermis with tetrodotoxin disrupted fear memory consolidation (Sacchetti et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sacchetti et al., 2002

claim: The cerebellum may be involved in the processing of aversive predictions and prediction errors.
source: Recent research argued that the cerebellum may be involved in the processing of aversive predictions and prediction errors, which has to be added to the neural network underlying emotional domain (Ernst et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ernst et al., 2019

claim: The cerebellum integrates multisensory information via Purkinje cells (PCs), the sole output of cerebellar cortex.
source: The cerebellum integrates multisensory information via Purkinje cells (PCs), the sole output of cerebellar cortex, and transfers the information to the cerebral cortex, brain stem, basal ganglia, and spinal cords (Adamaszek et al., 2017; Reeber et al., 2013; Frey et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Adamaszek et al., 2017; Reeber et al., 2013; Frey et al., 2011

claim: Parallel fibers (PFs) to PC synapses in the vermis lobule V/VI have been reported as a primary site for fear memory formation in the cerebellar cortex.
source: Parallel fibers (PFs) to PC synapses in the vermis lobule V/VI have been reported as a primary site for fear memory formation in the cerebellar cortex (Sacchetti et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sacchetti et al., 2004

claim: Auditory fear conditioning increased synaptic strength at PFs to PC synapses in the vermis lobule V/VI.
source: Auditory fear conditioning increased synaptic strength at PFs to PC synapses in the vermis lobule V/VI, and electrically induced long-term potentiation (LTP) in ex vivo slices was occluded after fear conditioning (Zhu et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhu et al., 2007

claim: Electrically induced long-term potentiation (LTP) in ex vivo slices was occluded after fear conditioning.
source: Auditory fear conditioning increased synaptic strength at PFs to PC synapses in the vermis lobule V/VI, and electrically induced long-term potentiation (LTP) in ex vivo slices was occluded after fear conditioning (Zhu et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhu et al., 2007

claim: GABAergic activity increases at molecular layer interneuron to PC synapses after fear conditioning.
source: It has also been known that GABAergic activity increases at molecular layer interneuron to PC synapses after fear conditioning (Scelfo et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Scelfo et al., 2008

claim: STAT3 regulates long-term depression (LTD) dependent on N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors (NMDA-Rs) in the hippocampus.
source: For example, STAT3 regulates long-term depression (LTD) dependent on N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors (NMDA-Rs) in the hippocampus (Nicolas et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nicolas et al., 2012

claim: JAK/STAT signaling pathway is involved in the synthesis of the brain's major ion channels and neurotransmitters.
source: Genomics research supported the involvement of JAK (Janus kinase)/STAT signaling pathway in the synthesis of the brain's major ion channels and neurotransmitters (Hixson et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hixson et al., 2019

claim: JAK/STAT signaling is involved in LTD at hippocampal temporoammonic-CA1 synapses.
source: JAK/STAT signaling is also involved in LTD at hippocampal temporoammonic-CA1 synapses (McGregor et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to McGregor et al., 2017

claim: JAKs can regulate the expression or function of γ-amino-butyric acid receptors (GABA-Rs) at inhibitory synapses.
source: At the inhibitory synapses, the JAKs can regulate the expression or function of γ-amino-butyric acid receptors (GABA-Rs) (Lund et al., 2008; Raible et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lund et al., 2008; Raible et al., 2015

claim: Activation of interleukin-6 receptors in the amygdala impaired auditory fear learning.
source: Furthermore, activation of interleukin-6 receptors which is an upstream regulator of STAT3 in the amygdala impaired auditory fear learning (Hao et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hao et al., 2014

claim: STAT3 expression in PCs was completely depleted in the lobule V/VI of STAT3PKO mice.
source: In the immunostaining assays, STAT3 expression in PCs was completely depleted in the lobule V/VI of STAT3PKO mice (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A,B

claim: STAT3PKO mice showed comparable expression levels of STAT3 to wild-type (WT) mice in the amygdala (BLA and CeA), hippocampus (CA3), and paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus.
source: We also confirmed that STAT3PKO mice showed comparable expression levels of STAT3 to wild-type (WT) mice in other brain regions critical for fear memory such as the amygdala (BLA and CeA), hippocampus (CA3), and paraventricular nucleus of the thalamus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D; Sanders et al., 2003; Ressler and Maren, 2019; Penzo et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D and citations to Sanders et al., 2003; Ressler and Maren, 2019; Penzo et al., 2015

claim: The gross morphology of PCs in STAT3PKO mice was similar to that in WT littermates.
source: In vitro live cell structural imaging with a calcium indicator revealed that the gross morphology of PCs in mutant mice was similar to that in WT littermates (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Deleting STAT3 did not affect dendritic branching processes in PCs.
source: The quantitative analysis of cerebellar dendritic arborization indicated that deleting STAT3 did not affect dendritic branching processes (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1D,E

claim: The number of dendritic spines showed no significant difference between WT and STAT3PKO mice.
source: Furthermore, the number of dendritic spines showed no significant difference between WT and STAT3PKO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E

claim: STAT3 depletion upregulated 1987 genes (5%) and downregulated 5039 genes (15%) in STAT3PKO mice compared to WT.
source: Differentially expressed gene (DEG) analysis indicated that among 34541 genes, STAT3 depletion upregulated 1987 genes (5%) and downregulated 5039 genes (15%) in STAT3PKO mice compared to WT (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by DEG analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: Upregulated genes in STAT3PKO mice were enriched in neuronal functions such as synaptic signaling and trans-synaptic signaling.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis showed the specific enrichment of upregulated genes in neuronal functions, such as synaptic signaling and trans-synaptic signaling, and the downregulated genes were enriched in GO terms related to G-protein receptor signaling and system processes (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 2B

claim: Downregulated genes in STAT3PKO mice were enriched in GO terms related to G-protein receptor signaling and system processes.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis showed the specific enrichment of upregulated genes in neuronal functions, such as synaptic signaling and trans-synaptic signaling, and the downregulated genes were enriched in GO terms related to G-protein receptor signaling and system processes (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 2B

claim: AMPA glutamate receptor complex was high ranked in GO analysis containing Gria1.
source: Interestingly, AMPA glutamate receptor complex was high ranked in GO analysis containing Gria1.
evidence: Supported by GO analysis results

claim: The amplitude of mEPSCs was significantly larger in STAT3PKO mice than in WT.
source: We found that the amplitude of mEPSCs was significantly larger in STAT3PKO mice than in WT, while the frequency of mEPSCs remained unchanged (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2E,F

claim: The frequency of mEPSCs remained unchanged between STAT3PKO and WT mice.
source: We found that the amplitude of mEPSCs was significantly larger in STAT3PKO mice than in WT, while the frequency of mEPSCs remained unchanged (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2E,F

claim: The frequency of mIPSCs was significantly smaller in STAT3PKO mice than in WT.
source: Unlike the excitatory synaptic transmission, the frequency of mIPSCs was significantly smaller in STAT3PKO mice than in WT, while the amplitude of mIPSCs remained unchanged (Figure 2H,I).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2H,I

claim: The amplitude of mIPSCs remained unchanged between STAT3PKO and WT mice.
source: Unlike the excitatory synaptic transmission, the frequency of mIPSCs was significantly smaller in STAT3PKO mice than in WT, while the amplitude of mIPSCs remained unchanged (Figure 2H,I).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2H,I

claim: HES1 and REST function as transcriptional repressors of AMPA-type glutamate receptor subunits 1 and 2 (GluA1 and GluA2).
source: Previous studies showed that Hes Family BHLH transcription factor 1 (HES1) and repressor element 1-silencing transcription factor (REST) function as transcriptional repressors of AMPA-type glutamate receptor subunits 1 and 2 (GluA1 and GluA2), respectively (Lin and Lee, 2012; Noh et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lin and Lee, 2012; Noh et al., 2012

claim: STAT3 is a transcription factor for HES1 and REST.
source: STAT3 is known as a transcription factor for HES1 and REST (Ma et al., 2010; Bedini et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ma et al., 2010; Bedini et al., 2008

claim: Hes1 and Rest expressions were reduced in STAT3PKO mice, while Gria1 and Gria2 were increased.
source: Our GO analysis indicated that Hes1 and Rest expressions were reduced in STAT3PKO mice, while Gria1 and Gria2 were increased (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 3A

claim: Hes1 and Rest mRNA expressions were significantly decreased in PC somas of STAT3PKO mice.
source: The Hes1 and Rest mRNA expressions were significantly decreased in PC somas; however, Gria1 and Gria2 expressions were significantly increased (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by mRNA expression data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Gria1 and Gria2 mRNA expressions were significantly increased in PC somas of STAT3PKO mice.
source: The Hes1 and Rest mRNA expressions were significantly decreased in PC somas; however, Gria1 and Gria2 expressions were significantly increased (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by mRNA expression data shown in Figure 3B

claim: There was no significant difference in the total amount of synaptic proteins (PSD95, GluA1/2, and CaMKII) between WT and STAT3PKO in cerebellar slices.
source: We found no significant difference in the total amount of these synaptic proteins between WT and STAT3PKO (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3C,D

claim: GluA1/2 expressions were significantly increased in the molecular layer of STAT3PKO mice compared to WT.
source: We found that GluA1/2 expressions were significantly increased in the molecular layer of STAT3PKO mice compared to WT (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3E,F

claim: Both protein and mRNA expressions of Gria1/2 were increased in STAT3-inhibited neurons.
source: In line with the RNA-seq analysis, we found that both protein and mRNA expressions of Gria1/2 were increased in STAT3-inhibited neurons, while mRNA expressions of Hes1 and Rest were decreased (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: mRNA expressions of Hes1 and Rest were decreased in STAT3-inhibited neurons.
source: In line with the RNA-seq analysis, we found that both protein and mRNA expressions of Gria1/2 were increased in STAT3-inhibited neurons, while mRNA expressions of Hes1 and Rest were decreased (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: The amplitude of eEPSCs in STAT3PKO mice was higher than that of eEPSCs in WT.
source: A comparison of the input–output curves of WT and KO in the baseline showed that the amplitude of eEPSCs in KO was higher than that of eEPSCs in WT (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3G

claim: No changes in either paired-pulse facilitation or depression were observed between WT and STAT3PKO mice.
source: We then calculated the paired-pulse ratio and observed no changes in either paired-pulse facilitation or depression (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3H

claim: Fear conditioning induced LTP of the PF to PC synapses and occluded further LTP in ex vivo slices.
source: Previous studies have shown that fear conditioning induced LTP of the PF to PC synapses and also occluded further LTP in ex vivo slices, suggesting that LTP might be a key cellular mechanism for fear memory formation (Sacchetti et al., 2004; Zhu et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sacchetti et al., 2004; Zhu et al., 2007

claim: Electrical stimulation of PF at 1 Hz induced LTP in WT mice, with AMPA-receptor-mediated EPSCs remaining potentiated for 50 min.
source: We electrically stimulated the PF at 1 Hz to induce LTP in WT. The AMPA-receptor-mediated EPSCs in WT mice remained potentiated for 50 min (Figure 3I).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3I

claim: The same stimulation protocol (1 Hz) induced LTD-like synaptic plasticity in STAT3PKO mice.
source: Interestingly, the same stimulation protocol induced LTD-like synaptic plasticity in STAT3PKO mice (Figure 3J).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3J

claim: Enhanced AMPA-R activity switches LTP to LTD in the cerebellar cortex.
source: Previous research has shown that enhanced AMPA-R activity switches LTP to LTD in the cerebellar cortex (van Beugen et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to van Beugen et al., 2014

claim: PC-specific STAT3 deletion did not impair the acquisition phase of auditory fear conditioning.
source: PC-specific STAT3 deletion did not impair the acquisition phase of auditory fear conditioning (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4A

claim: STAT3PKO mice displayed a comparable level of short-term fear memory to WT mice.
source: In contextual and cued fear conditioning, STAT3PKO mice displayed a comparable level of short-term fear memory to WT mice as assessed by freezing (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4B

claim: The long-term fear memory of STAT3PKO mice was significantly enhanced compared to WT mice only in the auditory cue test.
source: Interestingly, the long-term fear memory of STAT3PKO mice was significantly enhanced compared to the WT mice only in the auditory cue test (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Both WT and STAT3PKO mice did not show significant difference in the contextual memory test.
source: But both WT and STAT3PKO mice did not show significant difference in the contextual memory test (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4C

claim: The avoidance memory significantly increased in the STAT3PKO group after fear conditioning.
source: Next, we performed passive avoidance, fear-potentiated startle, and pre-pulse inhibition (PPI) tests (Figure 4D,E,F,G,H), and found that the avoidance memory significantly increased in the STAT3PKO group after fear conditioning (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4D

claim: STAT3PKO mice showed comparable startle reflex, including the auditory startle response and PPI, to WT mice.
source: The STAT3PKO mice showed comparable startle reflex, including the auditory startle response and PPI, to the WT mice (Figure 4E,G).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4E,G

claim: 24 hr after fear conditioning, STAT3PKO mice showed more exaggerated startle responses compared to WT group.
source: However, 24 hr after fear conditioning, the STAT3PKO mice showed more exaggerated startle responses compared to the WT group (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4F

claim: The number of jumps was not significantly different between WT and STAT3PKO mice.
source: By monitoring the video recordings, however, we analyzed the number of jumps was not significantly different between WT and STAT3PKO mice (Figure 4I).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4I

claim: STAT3PKO mice showed no significant difference in anxiety-like behavior in the elevated plus-maze tests compared to WT.
source: In addition, STAT3PKO mice showed no significant difference in anxiety-like behavior in the elevated plus-maze tests compared to WT (Figure 4J).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4J

claim: There was no correlation between PC-specific STAT3 expression and motor-related behaviors, including locomotor activity, motor coordination, and vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR).
source: We found no correlation between PC-specific STAT3 expression and motor-related behaviors, including locomotor activity, motor coordination, and vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) (Figure 4K,L,M).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4K,L,M

claim: Twenty-hours after fear conditioning, eEPSCs increased at PF to PC synapses of WT mice.
source: Twenty-hours after fear conditioning, eEPSCs increased at PF to PC synapses of WT mice as previously reported (Sacchetti et al., 2004; Figure 5A)
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5A and citation to Sacchetti et al., 2004

claim: Twenty-hours after fear conditioning, eEPSCs decreased in STAT3PKO mice.
source: Twenty-hours after fear conditioning, eEPSCs increased at PF to PC synapses of WT mice as previously reported (Sacchetti et al., 2004; Figure 5A); however, eEPSCs decreased in STAT3PKO mice (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5B

claim: PC-specific STAT3 deletion did not play a critical role in fear conditioning-induced potentiation at inhibitory synapses.
source: PC-specific STAT3 deletion did not play a critical role in fear conditioning-induced potentiation at inhibitory synapses.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from experimental observations

claim: LTP of inhibitory synapses was observed in both WT and STAT3PKO mice after fear conditioning.
source: LTP of inhibitory synapses was observed in both WT and STAT3PKO mice after fear conditioning (Figure 5D,E,F).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5D,E,F

claim: mIPSC frequency increased in both WT and STAT3PKO groups after fear conditioning.
source: In particular, mIPSC frequency increased in both WT and STAT3PKO groups after fear conditioning, as previously reported (Scelfo et al., 2008; Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5E and citation to Scelfo et al., 2008

claim: The spontaneous firing rate increased in WT mice after fear conditioning, but not in STAT3PKO mice.
source: The spontaneous firing rate increased in WT mice after fear conditioning, but not in STAT3PKO mice (Figure 5G,H).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5G,H

claim: Both the number of spikes and mean firing rate similarly increased in both WT and STAT3PKO groups when PCs were injected a series of increasing current steps at 100 pA intervals.
source: Both the number of spikes and mean firing rate similarly increased in both WT and STAT3PKO groups when PCs were injected a series of increasing current steps at 100 pA intervals (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B,C,D).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B,C,D

claim: The input resistance of STAT3PKO groups was higher than that of WT.
source: The analysis of the membrane properties of PCs showed that the input resistance of STAT3PKO groups was higher than that of WT (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E,F

claim: c-fos expressions were significantly increased in paraventricular nucleus of thalamus, basolateral amygdala, and prelimbic cortex in fear-conditioned STAT3PKO mice compared to conditioned WT mice.
source: Interestingly, we found that c-fos expressions were significantly increased in several fear-related areas, such as paraventricular nucleus of thalamus, basolateral amygdala, and prelimbic cortex, in the fear-conditioned STAT3PKO mice compared to conditioned WT mice (Figure 6A,B,C,D,E,F; Penzo et al., 2015; Silva et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6A,B,C,D,E,F and citations to Penzo et al., 2015; Silva et al., 2019

claim: c-fos expressions in hippocampus were increased in both WT and STAT3PKO mice after tone stimulation.
source: In addition, we confirmed that c-fos expressions in hippocampus were increased in both WT and STAT3PKO mice after tone stimulation.
evidence: Stated as a finding from experimental observations

claim: There was no difference of c-fos expressions in hippocampus between WT and STAT3PKO mice.
source: However, we did not find any difference of c-fos expressions between WT and STAT3PKO mice, suggesting that altered cerebellar synaptic plasticity may not affect hippocampal-dependent fear memory (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: Altered cerebellar synaptic plasticity may not affect hippocampal-dependent fear memory.
source: However, we did not find any difference of c-fos expressions between WT and STAT3PKO mice, suggesting that altered cerebellar synaptic plasticity may not affect hippocampal-dependent fear memory (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Inferred from the lack of difference in c-fos expression in hippocampus

claim: The depletion of STAT3 in PCs leads to differential expression of genes that regulate synaptic plasticity.
source: In sum, the transcriptome analyses suggest that deleting STAT3 in PCs leads to differential expression of genes that regulate synaptic plasticity.
evidence: Inferred from transcriptome analysis results

claim: The altered synaptic strength following the depletion of STAT3 might be attributed to the transcriptional regulation of synaptic plasticity-related genes.
source: These electrophysiological data suggest that the altered synaptic strength following the depletion of STAT3 might be attributed to the transcriptional regulation of synaptic plasticity-related genes.
evidence: Inferred from combined transcriptome and electrophysiology data

claim: The depletion of STAT3 enhances the expression of GluA1/2 by inhibiting the expression of HES1 and REST in PCs.
source: All things considered, these data suggest that the depletion of STAT3 enhances the expression of GluA1/2 by inhibiting the expression of HES1 and REST in PCs.
evidence: Inferred from combined molecular and expression data

claim: The deletion of STAT3 may alter the polarity of cerebellar synaptic plasticity.
source: These results indicate that the deletion of STAT3 may alter the polarity of cerebellar synaptic plasticity.
evidence: Inferred from LTP/LTD switching observations

claim: The ablation of STAT3 in PCs may be selectively involved in inducing long-term fear memory.
source: Taken together, the results indicate that the ablation of STAT3 in PCs may be selectively involved in inducing long-term fear memory.
evidence: Inferred from behavioral test results

claim: PC-specific STAT3 is not critically involved in the intrinsic excitability of PCs.
source: These data indicate that PC-specific STAT3 is not critically involved in the intrinsic excitability of PCs.
evidence: Inferred from intrinsic excitability measurements

claim: PC-specific STAT3 may activate a network of regions that mediate long-term fear memory consolidation.
source: Together, these results indicate that PC-specific STAT3 may activate a network of regions that mediate long-term fear memory consolidation.
evidence: Inferred from c-fos expression patterns across brain regions

claim: STAT3 physiologically maintains the fear memory network by controlling the cerebellar synaptic plasticity, preventing aberrant fear behavior.
source: In conclusion, we found that altered synaptic input strength in the STAT3PKO mice enhanced long-term fear memory. These results imply that STAT3 physiologically maintains the fear memory network by controlling the cerebellar synaptic plasticity, preventing aberrant fear behavior.
evidence: Inferred from combined behavioral and synaptic plasticity results

claim: Output strength in the PCs modulates the neural activity of highly interconnected areas that consist of fear memory network.
source: This study furthers the evidence that output strength in the PCs modulates the neural activity of highly interconnected areas that consist of fear memory network.
evidence: Inferred from combined electrophysiology and c-fos expression data

claim: STAT3 has a wide range of functions such as neuronal cell growth, survival, and differentiation.
source: Since STAT3 has a wide range of functions such as neuronal cell growth, survival, and differentiation (Levy and Darnell, 2002a; Di Domenico et al., 2010; Yadav et al., 2005), we further examined whether the ablation of STAT3 impaired cerebellar development.
evidence: Supported by citations to Levy and Darnell, 2002a; Di Domenico et al., 2010; Yadav et al., 2005

claim: Feedforward inhibition has been suggested as a neural circuitry mechanism for timing control in cerebellar fear conditioning.
source: In cerebellar fear conditioning, feedforward inhibition has been suggested as a neural circuitry mechanism for timing control (Sacchetti et al., 2009; Heiney et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sacchetti et al., 2009; Heiney et al., 2014

claim: Negative regulators play a functionally important role in synaptic plasticity and memory formation.
source: It is noteworthy that negative regulators play a functionally important role in synaptic plasticity and memory formation (Lee and Silva, 2009; Schoch and Abel, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lee and Silva, 2009; Schoch and Abel, 2014

claim: Suppressing the expression of memory-suppressing genes such as calcineurin was shown to enhance memory.
source: Suppressing the expression of memory-suppressing genes such as calcineurin was shown to enhance memory (Baumgärtel et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Baumgärtel et al., 2008

claim: Opening of VGCCs results in calcium influx, giving rise to an increase in the dendritic calcium concentration, which may lead to LTD induction rather than LTP.
source: Opening of VGCCs results in calcium influx, giving rise to an increase in the dendritic calcium concentration, which may lead to LTD induction rather than LTP (Ito, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ito, 2002

claim: Both excitatory and inhibitory synaptic plasticity are involved in freezing behavior.
source: To explain the functional consequence of the change in the polarity of synaptic plasticity, it is worth noting that both excitatory and inhibitory synaptic plasticity are involved in freezing behavior (Sacchetti et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sacchetti et al., 2009

claim: The activity of PCs is suppressed during a conditioned stimulus after eye blink conditioning.
source: In the case of eye blink conditioning, the activity of PCs is reported to be suppressed during a conditioned stimulus after conditioning (ten Brinke et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to ten Brinke et al., 2015

claim: The cerebellum has pathways to sensorimotor, associative, and modulatory forebrain.
source: Recently, it has been identified that the cerebellum has pathways to sensorimotor, associative, and modulatory forebrain (Pisano et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pisano et al., 2020

claim: Fear memory network is distributed in the forebrain.
source: As previous studies showed, fear memory network is distributed in the forebrain (Wager et al., 2015; Tovote et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wager et al., 2015; Tovote et al., 2015

claim: Cerebellar fastigial nucleus (FN)-ventrolateral periaqueductal grey (vlPAG) pathway is involved in the fear learning process.
source: In addition, cerebellar fastigial nucleus (FN)-ventrolateral periaqueductal grey (vlPAG) pathway is involved in the fear learning process (Frontera et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Frontera et al., 2020

claim: The suppression of DCN output facilitates freezing via reduction of activity in the vlPAG.
source: It has been suggested that the suppression of DCN output facilitates freezing via reduction of activity in the vlPAG (Vaaga et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vaaga et al., 2020

claim: Long-term fear memory could be understood as a small world network.
source: It has been argued that long-term fear memory could be understood as a small world network (Wheeler et al., 2013; Vetere et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wheeler et al., 2013; Vetere et al., 2017

claim: Inactivation of a single region disrupted the subcortical–cortical communication on global network organization.
source: Recent research suggests that inactivation of a single region disrupted the subcortical–cortical communication on global network organization (Grayson et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Grayson et al., 2016

claim: The cerebellum is progressively recognized for its cognitive role such as emotion.
source: The cerebellum is progressively recognized for its cognitive role such as emotion, as shown in previous human brain imaging and clinical reports (Stoodley and Schmahmann, 2009; Moberget et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Stoodley and Schmahmann, 2009; Moberget et al., 2018

claim: Psychiatric disorders may result from cerebellar dysfunctions.
source: Multiple animal studies also report that psychiatric disorders may result from cerebellar dysfunctions (Tsai et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tsai et al., 2012

claim: PTSD-related genes and signaling molecules have been predicted to act as memory enhancers or suppressors, particularly in the JAK2-STAT3 pathway.
source: PTSD-related genes and signaling molecules have long been predicted to act as memory enhancers or suppressors, particularly in the JAK2-STAT3 pathway (Mynard et al., 2004; Hauger et al., 2012; Daskalakis et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mynard et al., 2004; Hauger et al., 2012; Daskalakis et al., 2014

claim: STAT3 may act as a molecular switch to control fear behavior on the molecular and cellular basis of long-term fear memory storage.
source: Our findings suggest that STAT3 may act as a molecular switch to control fear behavior on the molecular and cellular basis of long-term fear memory storage.
evidence: Inferred from combined molecular, cellular, and behavioral findings

claim: STAT3PKO mice showed the enhancement of long-term memory not only in Pavlovian fear conditioning but also in avoidance memories and fear-potentiated responses.
source: STAT3PKO mice showed the enhancement of long-term memory not only in Pavlovian fear conditioning but also in avoidance memories and fear-potentiated responses, which were less relevant to purely motor-related behaviors (Figure 4).

claim: STAT3PKO mice was shown to be normal on cerebellum-dependent motor learning.
source: Interestingly, STAT3PKO mice was shown to be normal on cerebellum-dependent motor learning.

claim: Deletion of STAT3 in flocculus might not affect the induction of synaptic plasticity for motor learning.
source: One possible explanation is that deletion of STAT3 in flocculus might not affect the induction of synaptic plasticity for motor learning.

claim: Rest is expressed in vermis lobule V/VI, but rarely expressed in the flocculus.

claim: Lack of Rest expression may limit the effect of STAT3 deletion on the induction of synaptic plasticity in the flocculus and VOR learning.
source: Lack of Rest expression may limit the effect of STAT3 deletion on the induction of synaptic plasticity in the flocculus and VOR learning.
evidence: Speculative explanation based on Rest expression patterns

claim: The STAT3PKO mice can be proposed as the suitable genetic model to study cerebellar synaptic plasticity in relation to traumatic event-related psychiatric disorders.
source: Thus, the STAT3PKO mice can be proposed as the suitable genetic model to study cerebellar synaptic plasticity in relation to traumatic event-related psychiatric disorders.
